item.title: Weeds or Medicine? What Our Elders Knew About Mental Health
item.description:
Gut-Brain Axis

Weeds or Medicine? What Our Elders Knew About Mental Health

How pot likker and field greens became mental health support.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Dandelion greens contain prebiotic fiber that feeds the gut microbiome and directly supports mental health.
  • The gut and brain are in constant conversation; what we eat shapes our mental health.
  • Adolescence is a critical window when diet shapes brain development, emotional regulation, and resilience.
  • Black elders practicing food as medicine were doing what nutritional psychiatry is only now confirming.
The Home Pharmacy
Source: Arletha Lizana

I was a child the first time my grandmother sent me to a field near our apartment in Pittsburgh.

It was not a cute, manicured garden; it was a literal field, the kind of overgrown, sun-baked stretch of land that most people walked past without a second glance. She handed me a paper bag and pointed. Go pick dandelion greens. And don’t come back with just a little bit. She said it the way she said everything—with the quiet authority of someone who knew exactly what she was doing, even when you had no idea why.

I complained, as children do. But I picked the greens. I brought them home. She washed them, cooked them down into her collard greens, and set a plate in front of me, like she had just done something completely ordinary. She had. She had also just given me medicine. She just didn’t call it that. I had to eat every ounce of what she gave me and drink the pot liquor (likker).

Generations of Accumulated Wisdom

Our elders didn’t use the phrase gut-brain axis. They never read a study on psychobiotics or prebiotic fiber and mental health outcomes in adolescents. But they knew, in the way many Black elders just know things, through generations of accumulated wisdom passed down person to person, that what you put in your body changes how you feel, how you think, how you move through the world. They knew that food was not just fuel. It was healing. They knew food is medicine. And they made sure we got our portion of it, whether we wanted to go pick it or not. How many of you grew up forcing down the liver and onions your grandmother made you eat?

That weed in the field is not a weed. Dandelion has been used as medicine across cultures for centuries in West African herbal traditions, in Chinese medicine, in indigenous North American practice, in European folk healing. Enslaved Africans arriving in the American South recognized dandelion growing wild in the fields and incorporated it into their healing practices, just as they braided seeds into their hair and carried botanical knowledge across the Middle Passage. According to the Black Food Canon, dandelion was gathered as a field green across the South, wilted in pot likker, and used medicinally as a liver-supporting, digestion-stimulating bitter. It was not a weed. It was part of a pharmacy growing at the edge of the yard. There are so many others, including red clover and plantain.

Prebiotic Fiber and a Healthy Mind

Modern science has confirmed what our ancestors practiced. Dandelion greens are rich in prebiotic fiber, the kind that feeds beneficial bacteria in the gut, as well as vitamins A, C, and K; iron; calcium; and potent antioxidants. They support liver function, reduce inflammation, and improve gut motility. But here is the connection our elders did not state, but our generation needs to hear: A healthy gut is the foundation of a healthy mind.

The gut is the second brain. The gut-brain axis is one of the most rapidly advancing areas in mental health science. Researchers describe it as a bidirectional communication network linking the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system through the vagus nerve, neurotransmitters, immune signals, and microbial metabolites. In plain language, your gut and your brain are in constant conversation. The health of one shapes the health of the other. The gut microbiome, the ecosystem of bacteria living in your digestive system, turns out to be one of the most powerful influencers of mood, cognition, anxiety, and depression we have ever identified.

Nutrition in Adolescence

The implications for young people are especially significant. Research in Translational Psychiatry found that adolescence is a critical window when the gut-brain axis is actively being fine-tuned, meaning that dietary interventions during this period may produce long-lasting consequences for mental health, for better or worse. What a young person eats during adolescence is not just shaping their body; it is shaping their brain, their emotional regulation, and their resilience. Studies consistently show that gut microbiome disruption is associated with greater depression and anxiety symptoms in children and adolescents. And diets high in prebiotic fiber, the kind found in dandelion greens, collards, and the full range of foods that stocked Black Southern kitchens, are directly linked to improved mental health outcomes.

Our ancestors were doing precision mental health intervention; they just called it supper. The philosophy of food as medicine has deep roots in Black culture, stretching from West African food traditions through the survival kitchens of enslaved people to the Sunday dinner tables of the South. Enslaved Africans brought with them botanical knowledge—of roots, leaves, and herbs that sustained bodies and spirits through unimaginable conditions. Dark leafy greens, including collards, mustard greens, and dandelion, were used not just as sustenance but as tools of detoxification, immune support, and healing. The pot likker left behind after a slow cook of greens—that deeply concentrated, vitamin-rich broth that Black Southern grandmothers swore by—was medicine passed down in a pot.

Modernity's Price on Mental Health

Somewhere along the way, we began to see these traditions as old-fashioned, as poverty food, as things to leave behind on the way to modernity. We traded the field greens for processed food. We traded the slow-cooked pot for the fast-food drive-through. And our children, inheriting disrupted microbiomes and an unsupportive food system, are paying the price in their mental health.

I’m not saying a bowl of greens can replace clinical care, or that dandelion tea cures depression or a plate of collards replaces therapy. The youth mental health crisis demands systemic responses: more culturally affirming providers, better funding, greater access, and genuine investment in Black children’s well-being. But I am saying that we have underestimated how much damage we did when we walked away from the food traditions our elders built and how much healing is available to us if we walk back toward them. Nutritional psychiatry is now a recognized field. The research on diet and youth mental health is compelling and growing. Our elders were practicing it before it had a name.

Go pick some greens. The act of sending a child to the field is not just about the greens. It's about being in the earth, feeling the sun, bringing something back with your own hands that would feed the table. That act alone—the going outside, the bending down, the gathering, the returning—is the kind of embodied, nature-connected practice that research now tells us supports mental health in young people. Our elders were giving us prebiotic fiber, and they were giving us grounding. They were feeding our gut and our sense of belonging to something larger than ourselves.

item.title: The In-Between: Covert Consciousness
item.description:
Consciousness

The In-Between: Covert Consciousness

The brain’s boundary between consciousness and unconsciousness.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Some patients who appear unconscious may still be consciously aware of their surroundings.
  • Specialized EEG and fMRI can sometimes reveal covert consciousness missed at the bedside.
  • Locked-in syndrome can leave a person fully conscious despite near-total paralysis.
Source: Merrilee Schultz / Unsplash

Is it possible for someone to appear to be in a deep coma, paralyzed, yet have a brain that is silently aware of all that’s going on around them?

Yes. This condition is called “locked-in syndrome,” which is an extreme example of the dichotomy of having a totally paralyzed body (except for the eyes), but an awake, perfectly conscious brain and mind.

But there are other, perhaps less well-known, medical conditions that result in a state of “semi-consciousness;” states that result from a variety of brain injuries, like stroke or head trauma, that persist sometimes for many weeks, even years.

These are called the Vegetative State (or, more correctly now, the Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome-UWS) and The Minimally Conscious State-MCS.

Before discussing these fascinating neurological states, to address the question, “What is consciousness?”: I believe it depends on who is offering its meaning. Neurologists, like me, will describe it as a state of being aware of one’s environment, including one’s inner environment of the “self.” Philosophers will have a different definition: consciousness is what it feels like from the inside, what constitutes “intentionality,” how we engage with the world.

In my Neurological ICU, we assess “consciousness,” or “awareness,” by asking our patients to follow commands: Give me a thumbs up. Open your eyes. Our nurses ask this every hour on the hour, as part of their around-the-clock neurological examination. The ability to follow commands will often be our first indication that someone is coming out of a coma, our first glimpse of recovery.

But if our patient cannot follow commands at the bedside, this doesn’t necessarily mean they are unaware, or unconscious. “Cognitive Motor Dissociation” is a state of disordered consciousness in which a person will not demonstrate brain activity by following commands at the bedside but is able to do so covertly. For example, a person who cannot visibly respond to commands will be able to perform a requested mental task, such as imagining lifting a finger, or playing tennis, when they are receiving specialized neurotechnology such as task-based electroencephalograms (EEGs) or functional MRI scans.

Source: Alexander Grey / Unsplash

Patients who have been treated as unarousable or comatose are shown to actually “be there” by these specialized tests. Unfortunately, most of this technology is still primarily reserved for research studies at academic medical centers and is not readily available at the bedside.

So, it’s frightening to think that a patient in an apparent unconscious state has been aware all along: when their arm is caught under them while being turned, while people are speaking about their prognosis at their bedside, and they can’t object or ask questions—when they are unable to cry out or grimace or express what’s going on in their head.

After severe brain injury or illness, people don’t usually stay in a coma (from the Greek “koma,” deep sleep) very long; generally two to four weeks. If they survive, they progress to one of the “in-between” states of Unresponsive Wakefulness State or Minimally Conscious State, and then, hopefully, wake up. Some never wake up. People in the UWS retain the vegetative functions of the body, like digestion, cardiac and respiratory function, so they don’t necessarily need to be on a ventilator, and they have normal sleep-wake cycles. People in the MCS are moving closer to consciousness, although their awareness and interactions with us and their environment are inconsistent… reflecting isolated areas of cortical connectivity. Full consciousness, on the other hand, requires sustained integration of cortical nerve cell activity throughout the brain.

Source: Venti Views / Unsplash

These in-between states can be difficult to distinguish from the “locked-in syndrome,” in which patients are paralyzed, but preserve the ability to move the eyes and to blink. Patients can look up and down and can blink to command. So, they consistently and correctly answer questions by these movements. Locked-in syndrome can occur from tumors, strokes or demyelinating diseases that knock out the ventral pons in the brainstem. The cortex above remains intact. Patients are quadriplegic, their face is paralyzed, they often cannot breathe on their own, and they can lose the all-important brainstem reflexes that permit us to cough and swallow.

Yet these patients are fully conscious. The French journalist Jean-Dominique Bauby, who at 43, suffered a pontine stroke that left him alert, but locked-in, wrote his memoir The Diving Bell and the Butterfly by painstakingly dictating one letter at a time using only his left eyelid and a code written down by his partner at his bedside. The book took about 200,000 blinks to write. Remarkable. Bauby died of pneumonia in 1997, just two days after the book was published in France.

Today, we can offer locked-in patients a way to communicate their invisible thoughts with brain-computer interface systems that allow them to select a letter through a detectable brain signal via scalp EEG or implanted cortical electrodes.

What these remarkable patients have taught me is to never assume unconsciousness. Instead, assume the best: that the person in front of me in the ICU is invisibly conscious and aware of all we are saying. They can hear what their families and their visiting friends are saying to them. And I tell each patient on rounds every day what the day will hold, how they’re doing, what we plan next.

If I am wrong, and they are completely unconscious, no harm done. If I am right, whether proven by a task-based EEG or functional MRI scan, or better yet, by their waking up one day, those days and weeks have not been spent in stillness and stupor.

They have not been alone.

item.title: Why Fighting Against Social Anxiety Could Be Making It Worse
item.description:
Anxiety

Why Fighting Against Social Anxiety Could Be Making It Worse

Counterintuitively, turning toward anxiety could make it less distressing.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Social anxiety is worry about what others think of you.
  • Social anxiety is composed of both thoughts and physical sensations, which are interlinked.
  • Bracing against social anxiety can create feedback loops that may make it worse.
Social anxiety: worry about what others think of you
Source: Yan Krukov / Pexels

When we feel ourselves getting socially anxious, our knee-jerk reaction is often to try to avoid it. But if we welcome it in, the effect can be quite different from what we expect.

What Is Social Anxiety?

Most people have felt socially anxious at one time or another. Think about what’s going through your mind before giving a speech, during an important job interview, or, really, any situation where you worry about what others might think of you.

In addition to—and indeed connected to—these in-the-moment thoughts, there are physical sensations: butterflies in the stomach, trembling, or a dry mouth, to name but a few. When I interviewed socially anxious women as part of my research (Masters, 2024), many spoke about blushing and sweating (Farah*), while others described feeling nauseous (Daniella).

Mind, Body, and Feedback Loops

Feedback loops in social anxiety: is there another way?
Source: Marcos Sánchez / Pexels

It might be tempting to think of social anxiety as having mental and physical aspects, and it’s likely so difficult to get away from this because we don’t really have a word—in common usage, at least—that conveys that we’re talking about the whole self.

Yet, thinking about the mental and the physical as existing independently might not be that helpful (despite what mind-body dualist philosopher Descartes would have us believe!), especially in this context. Another woman I interviewed, Amy, was herself pretty critical of the notion that the mind and body are distinct, calling it "a fallacy." Instead, Amy advocated for a more integrated or biopsychosocial view. An article by the Royal College of Psychiatrists (2016) explains this rather nicely in the case of social anxiety—that is, how emotions affect the body, and vice versa:

"Other people may be able to see some of the signs of this anxiety—the blushing, stammering, shaking and trembling.

These symptoms can be quite alarming and make your anxiety worse. It can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

You worry so much about looking worried that you actually do look worried."

What we have here is a feedback loop being set up: You worry about what others think of you; you exhibit some of the physical signs of social anxiety; you then worry that others can see these signs and they’ll think badly of you; the social anxiety becomes worse; the physical symptoms are exacerbated; and so on.

Breaking the Cycle: Laying Out the Welcome Mat for It

The key to breaking this feedback loop could lie, counterintuitively, not in trying to prevent these physical manifestations, but in doing the opposite: embracing them. By way of example, those among you who are prone to blushing: Has there ever been a time when you’ve successfully managed to stop blushing simply by willing your cheeks to be less red, or trying really, really hard not to? Or have these strategies instead made the blushing worse?

The idea of turning toward, instead of turning away from, difficult sensations or emotions has its roots in some branches of meditation or mindfulness. I first came across this as part of my own journey in working through the book Overcoming Worry and Generalised Anxiety Disorder a few years ago. In the appendices, psychologists Mark Freeston and Kevin Meares signpost the reader to mindfulness, in particular citing Jon Kabat-Zinn and Mark Williams as names the reader might want to look up.

One of the key tenets of mindfulness is acceptance: that is, letting go of the tendency that we have to want things to be different from how they are. Alongside this, Jon Kabat-Zinn (2023) often advocates putting out the welcome mat for, or letting in, difficult experiences, such as emotional distress or physical pain.

Laying out the welcome mat: turning toward difficult emotions or sensations rather than shying away from them
Source: Andrew Neel / Pexels

Freeston and Meares themselves espouse a strategy akin to this in their book on generalised anxiety disorder, wherein they suggest the reader writes down their worries and sets aside some time later in their day especially to "have a good worry." The thinking here is that, with the attention lasered in on the worry, the worry dissolves: a bit like looking under your bed and seeing the proverbial monster—it’s far less scary than you thought when viewed head-on instead of catching mere glimpses of it.

Applying this to social anxiety, let’s say you become embarrassed. Your default reaction might be, "Oh no, I’m blushing and sweating, and my voice is trembling." Then you start to worry that people notice, which makes it (the blushing et al.) worse, and so forth—exactly as we saw in the Royal College of Psychiatrists’ article.

So how do we break this feedback loop? An alternative to resisting or bracing against these experiences could lie in embracing them, or welcoming them in. Next time you feel yourself becoming socially anxious, what happens if you lean into it—to whatever extent you’re comfortable doing so—and are curious about it? What are the sensations like? Exactly where are they? What qualities (shape/texture/temperature) do they have? What are the thoughts? Are they coming and going? How are they making themselves known? And how is all of this changing with time?

Following Freeston and Meares, what we’re doing here could be described not as letting ourselves "have a good worry," but as letting ourselves "have a good old experience of social anxiety." And while we may not be able to rid ourselves completely of the social anxiety itself (and all of its associated physical sensations)—at least not right away—letting it be there, instead of pushing it away, can be a very different, and perhaps less distressing, experience. As Kabat-Zinn (2019) has written in relation to dealing with life's difficulties: "You can’t stop the waves, but you can learn to surf."

*Names have been changed to protect anonymity

item.title: The Benefits of Having an Older Sibling During Adolescence
item.description:
Adolescence

The Benefits of Having an Older Sibling During Adolescence

Older siblings can serve as positive role models and guides for teens.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Older siblings can serve as a trusted resource for support, information, and help for teenagers.
  • Younger siblings can benefit from older siblings’ knowledge and experience with friends, school, and dating.
  • A close relationship with an older sibling is associated with teenagers’ greater well-being.
Source: tetesong / Shutterstock

Adolescence is an important time when young people seek independence from their parents, focusing on friends and romantic partners and figuring out who they want to be. As teens navigate these important developmental tasks, they will learn and grow with the help of others. For adolescents with an older sibling, that sibling can be an important, trusted family resource who helps guide them during this developmental period.

While siblings do spend less time together during adolescence, they remain an important and influential relationship for youths' social, emotional, and cognitive development. In fact, adolescents report sharing and discussing personal information and thoughts with their siblings daily. Although older siblings are not always a positive influence, they can play a beneficial role in the lives of younger siblings during adolescence.

Older Siblings as an Important Family Resource

In the United States, most siblings are about two years apart in age, creating likely similarities in their life experiences. These similarities, along with siblings’ shared family history and special understanding of one another, can make an older sibling an ideal resource during adolescence. A sibling can also provide an alternative source of support for youth who may not feel comfortable talking to their parents or need a different perspective.

Teens may also seek out their older siblings as relatable confidants, perhaps using them as a sounding board before approaching their parents or other adults. Adolescents may enjoy the back-and-forth conversation with their sibling more than top-down pressure from parents. Reflecting this trust, research shows that adolescent siblings frequently talk about their daily activities, media use, nonfamilial relationships, academics, and future plans.

During adolescence, sibling support is often mutual, especially when navigating family matters. However, older siblings generally have more influence on younger siblings than vice versa, often adopting a teacher or mentor role even if they are only a few years older. Younger siblings often admire and look up to their older siblings. This status typically happens because of birth order and age: Older siblings are likely to face social situations with peers and romantic partners, encounter academic challenges and classes, and make decisions about future plans before their younger siblings.

Having Older Sisters Versus Older Brothers

Does it matter if an adolescent has an older brother or sister? The findings are mixed, with some studies showing no effect. Other studies show that younger siblings receive more guidance and support from same-sex rather than opposite-sex older siblings. This is thought to happen because same-sex siblings share greater similarities and relate to each other more easily. Additionally, older sisters are often close confidants and mentors for younger sisters and provide more advice than older brothers do. For example, one study found that older sisters give younger sisters specific instructions and information about dating and romantic relationships.

How Older Siblings Benefit Younger Siblings

Older siblings can influence adolescent younger siblings in several ways, including by guiding them through direct instruction and encouragement or by providing information and advice. Another way older siblings influence younger siblings is by serving as role models. By watching their older siblings’ activities, choices, and subsequent consequences, younger siblings learn from them.

Older brothers and sisters are invaluable guides promoting positive development for their less experienced younger siblings in a variety of areas, including dating and peer relationships, body image, and prosocial skills like empathy. One study showed that older siblings shape adolescents’ social skills and their athletic and artistic interests, particularly when older siblings excelled in those areas. Other work found that how much adolescents discussed extracurricular activities, media, and academics with their older siblings was linked to their success in friendships, sports, and school.

Tips to Foster the Benefits of Adolescent Older Siblings

Parents can encourage strong, loving sibling relationships in which older siblings serve as positive role models and resources for younger siblings during adolescence through the following suggestions:

  • Encourage your children to talk directly to one another about both their joys and challenges.
  • Understand that, at times, siblings may fight or need space from one another.
  • Model and encourage siblings to use constructive conflict management strategies (e.g., listening and developing and choosing solutions together).
  • Privately coach siblings to find simple ways to show empathy when their sibling is having a difficult time.
  • Nurture siblings’ connections with one another through their shared activities, routines, and interests.
  • Encourage siblings’ support of one another’s accomplishments, hobbies, and talents rather than feelings of competition.

item.title: Beyond 'Forgive and Forget': 5 Practical Relationship Habits
item.description:
Relationships

Beyond 'Forgive and Forget': 5 Practical Relationship Habits

Five habits for a healthier, more connected relationship.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • The opposite of forgiveness is resentment.
  • Acknowledge what happened, learn from it, forgive, and let it go.
  • Truly, completely accept your partner as they are.
Strong relationships grow through generosity, acceptance, and the willingness to let go of resentment.
Source: Jason Leung / Unsplash

In an era dominated by relationship burnout and hyper-individualism, many couples find themselves trapped in endless cycles of friction and emotional distance. Breaking free requires adopting habits that run counter to modern culture. Here are some counterintuitive relationship habits you could consider adopting or adapting to fit the unique rhythm and idiosyncrasies of your (current or future) intimate relationship.

Never think less of yourself; often think of yourself less

Life is a process of displacement. When you are born, you immediately become #1. As long as you are single, you remain #1—it’s still about you and your freedom.

When you get married, you become #2. You have to learn to put your spouse first (without compromising your deeply held values—that’s why choosing the right person is the most important decision you’ll ever make) if you want the marriage to work.

When you have a child, you become #3. By the time you become a grandparent, you’re lucky if you’re still in the Top 10.

While it sounds like you become weaker, it’s the opposite: You become stronger. While it sounds like you become a follower, it’s, again, the opposite: This is true leadership. The front-stage star is not a leader, but a showman—not the director, but an actor.

The true leader is the one you don’t see, the back-stage architect whose undying devotion enables the unfolding drama, which involves many, to captivate and enthrall, night after night.

Just give

Twenty-five years ago, I was wrestling with my inner demons about commitment and went on a walk along the Potomac River outside of Washington, DC, with a close family friend who had been married to his wife for more than 40 years.

“How have you managed being married for so long?” I asked him.

Robert looked at the turbulent rapids and thought for a while. Then he said, “The best advice I ever received was from my aunt, while I was fixing my tuxedo just before Charlene and I were married.”

He had my attention. “What did she say?”

“She said, ‘Robert, always remember this: Whatever Charlene does, just give. No matter what happens, always give. And the two of you will be fine.’”

I’ll pass on Robert’s aunt’s sage advice: Just give. No matter what. It’s your only power. You control how, when, and what to give.

What you receive, on the other hand, is completely out of your control. Yet the more and better you give, the more love will also come in your direction.

Don’t build a case

In other words, let things go. There are two things you do in life: You choose how you want to live, and you live with what you choose.

You chose a long-term commitment to this person, which means letting lots of things (but not everything) go. Consider that the opposite of forgiveness is resentment. A word derived from the Latin roots re (again) and sentire (to feel), resentment is to feel anger again and again until you become paralyzed.

Forgiveness is a better option: while resentment paralyzes, forgiveness liberates.

Forgiveness releases us from the past without asking us to forget it.
Source: Stepan / Unsplash

Don’t forgive and forget

As children, we’re often told by adults—generally with good intentions—to “forgive and forget.” To forget, however, may not be the best idea.

If you fall into a ditch, the last thing you want to do is forget the location of the ditch. Such a strategy may result in your falling in again.

A better way to approach forgiveness is to acknowledge what the other person did, file it away, give for the other person to yourself, and then let it go. This approach need not include your tolerating the same behavior again.

Forgiveness, in fact, does not necessarily lead to a continued relationship. In many cases, forgiveness enables you to detach yourself from the relationship, not only physically but also emotionally and psychologically.

Importantly, while trust binds, forgiveness releases. While forgiveness is needed for personal development, trust is needed for relational development.

Trust is not necessarily an evolutionary adaptive behavior, as it can lead to more harmful behavior from the other person. A man can apologize to his wife for an affair, for example, regain her trust, and then continue to cheat on her afterward.

While trusting a specific person whom you feel has harmed you is not necessary for your evolution as a human being, forgiving them is. Forgiveness is one of your most critical attributes because until you let go of your suffering, you don’t let it recede from the present and into the past.

Until you forgive and then learn to love any person in your life, you remain trapped in a drama with them. You remain on their stage, entangled in an invisible thread that binds you to them.

You may be acting out the drama with the surrogates you bring into your life to replace them, but you are still cast in the role. This is how love liberates, how love sets you free.

Truly, completely accept your partner as they are

The more you are able to take this cognitive step toward understanding and respecting innate differences that will always be beyond your control, the more inner peace and happiness you will invite into your life.

If you are like most of us, you probably have not yet made this transformative decision. You have likely spent most of your life preoccupied with the comings and goings and machinations and preferences of the other characters in your story—including and especially your partner—instead of seeing them as they are: as other human beings who enter and exit your stage throughout your life.

How can you accept yourself and others as you and they are while also retaining your optimism about what you and they can become?

item.title: Narrative and Illness: The Autobiographical Stories We Tell Matter
item.description:
Chronic Illness

Narrative and Illness: The Autobiographical Stories We Tell Matter

As identity is changed by illness, how do we work with our narrative to reflect this?

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Narratives about self shape the actuality of our lives.
  • Attention to narrative elements like character, theme, and perspective can sharpen our life stories.
  • Therapy can be a space for creating and editing autobiographical narrative.
Source: Katie Willard Virant

Humans love stories. From oral storytelling to novels to movies and television—we make sense of our world through narrative. Through stories, we seek to understand ourselves and be understood by others. Stories are especially important in identity construction. That is, we define ourselves in large part by the narrative we tell about who we are. As identity is profoundly changed by illness, how do we work with our narrative to reflect this shift?

Illness and narrative choices

For most people, illness is a “biographical disruption.” It’s an unexpected and often devastating event that blows up life as we’ve known it. We become acquainted with pain, fear, loneliness, and limitations. The people we were before illness could count on our bodies to work. The people we were before illness understood suffering as an abstract concept rather than as a lived experience. The people we were before illness had freedom in moving through the world that we took entirely for granted.

When illness strikes, we experience deep grief. We mourn for the things we have lost, especially our pre-illness identity. The grief is necessary, as we can never be who we once were. As we go through the grief process, we have to make a narrative decision: Is illness the end of our story, or is there a way our story can continue?

In their article “Volition as Narrative: Understanding Motivation in Chronic Illness,” Helfrich, Kielhofner, & Mattingly (1994) describe two people whose lives have been interrupted by serious illness. One individual continues to fight for his lifelong dream of being a reporter. He’s had to reconceptualize what this will look like. While he may never write for a prestigious national publication, he finds ways to continue reporting for smaller outlets, pivoting as needed. He says, “[P]eople who don’t get sick make [long-term] plans. Every plan that I’ve made has eventually been defeated and I’ve had to shift to another subplan.” But he keeps shifting, as many times as he needs to. He keeps writing more chapters of his life story.

The other case study in the article describes a woman who has not been able to make a meaningful life for herself post-illness. She says, “I feel like I got cheated out of my life.” In contrast to the first case study, her story ended with illness. No further chapters were written.

The narrative concept of “character”

One important narrative concept is “character.” How often do we read or watch a story and remark on the characters presented? While the events that occur in a story are certainly important, the intersection of plot with character is what makes stories so meaningful. In the article discussed above, for example, the reporter is a richly developed character. He is smart, determined, and resourceful. He is resilient. His sense of himself as a character with these traits enables him to meet the plot twist in his story with the strengths he believes himself to possess.

If I were working with the woman in the article, I’d want to get a sense of who she imagines herself to be as a character in her own life story. I’m guessing she may never have thought about herself in this way. I would ask her to tell me what she was like as a kid: What did she enjoy playing? Who did she enjoy playing with? I would ask her to tell me what she wanted for herself prior to illness and what she hopes for herself now. I would ask her to tell me what traits she values in herself and in others. I would ask her to flesh out for me who she is as a character in her own story. Undoubtedly, we would discover character traits we could build upon, strengths that might guide her as she imagines continuing her narration post-illness.

The narrative concept of “other characters”

Another important narrative concept is “other characters.” Stories typically involve characters interacting with other characters. In the article, the reporter mentions the support his mother gave him. By contrast, the woman speaks of an interaction with a doctor in which he told her that her illness would prevent her from ever finishing college. As in novels and films, other people are tremendously important in our life stories. In our own stories, who are the characters that support us, that help us along the way? Who are the characters who cut us down and make our lives feel smaller and harder? How can we invite in supportive characters while minimizing the damage done by non-supportive characters?

The narrative concept of listeners

“Narratives are created between people” (Ellis-Hill, Payne, & Ward, 2008). A novel has readers. A movie has watchers. A story has listeners. We create stories because we want to be seen and understood. We listen to stories because we want to see and understand. What is the story you want to tell about your life? Who do you want to listen?

Therapy as narration boot camp

If you’ve never thought about your life story, or if your life story needs a rewrite, therapy is a great place to do this work. Like an editor, therapists can often see elements of a story that the writer can’t. We can help you identify threads of meaning that run through your story (themes), and we can help you view your story in different ways (perspectives). Most importantly, we can help you with the chapter you are writing right now, in the present. What do you want this chapter to look like? Who can you imagine yourself to be in these unchosen circumstances? It’s your story: What are you going to write?

item.title: A Forgotten Remedy for Depression
item.description:
Depression

A Forgotten Remedy for Depression

Putting exercise back on the map as a means of managing depression.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Exercise can be as effective as antidepressants, and some studies suggest it may be even more effective.
  • Most mental health professionals have received no formal training in prescribing exercise to treat depression.
  • A simple framework, FITT, can help people get started and design an exercise routine that works for them.
Source: Pexels/Polina Tankilevitch

There’s growing concern about the risks of antidepressants, including side effects and withdrawal symptoms. Many people who are taking antidepressants are now turning to deprescribing resources, while others who are experiencing depression are wondering whether they should start taking antidepressants at all or if there’s another way.

But there’s one remedy that hasn’t gotten the attention it deserves: exercise.

In what follows, I’ll look at the surprising antidepressant effects of exercise, why it isn’t prescribed more widely, and a simple framework to help people get started.

Exercise Is as Effective as Antidepressants

One of the most astonishing findings in recent depression research is that exercise can be as effective as antidepressants, and some studies suggest it may be even more effective for mild to moderate depression. Millions of people have been prescribed powerful psychiatric drugs, often without being told that something as ordinary as walking, jogging, cycling, or strength training might provide comparable benefits.

The evidence has become increasingly difficult to ignore. Exercise ranks as one of the most effective known lifestyle interventions for depression. These include aerobic exercises, walking, jogging, strength training, and yoga. Intriguingly, evidence suggests that strength training is slightly more effective for women and younger adults, and yoga for men and older adults.

Exercise isn't just about shedding calories. It improves inflammation, metabolism, sleep, and the body's response to stress. These are precisely the factors that can go wrong in depression. But I think there's something deeper going on.

I've argued that depression may be a functional signal: our brain's way of telling us that something in our lives isn't going well and needs more attention. Sometimes the problem is a relationship, a job, or a life goal that no longer suits us. But sometimes the problem is the way we're living.

Humans evolved to move. Our ancestors spent much of their days walking, gathering food, carrying things, and engaging physically with the world. They didn't spend eight hours sitting in front of a computer, followed by another four hours staring at a smartphone. Yet that's how many of us live today.

Is it surprising that our bodies, and our minds, are protesting? Perhaps depression is telling us that something is wrong with the lives we've built for ourselves.

Why Isn't Exercise Prescribed More for Depression?

The evidence for the benefits of exercise is strong enough that a group of psychiatrists recently asked, in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, whether failing to prescribe exercise for depression could amount to “psychiatric malpractice.”

Part of the problem, they argue, is training. In one survey, 92 percent of mental health professionals said they'd received no formal training in prescribing exercise, and 41 percent said they never prescribe it at all.

Still, simply telling people to “be active” rarely works. People who struggle with depression need guidance and support.

The FITT Framework: Designing an Exercise Program to Treat Depression

For those for whom exercise is a real possibility, the same group offers a simple framework called FITT, which stands for frequency, intensity, time, and type. As a rule of thumb (and obviously to be adjusted for each person's physical health and other medical conditions):

  • Frequency: Three to five sessions a week
  • Intensity: Moderate to vigorous (brisk walking, cycling, swimming)
  • Time: 45 to 60 minutes per session
  • Type: Aerobic, strength training, or mind-body practices like yoga—whichever you're most likely to keep doing

But they also emphasize that less is better than none. Even one or two sessions a week, or 10 to 30 minutes at a time, can help.

Sometimes, what depression may be pointing to is precisely the mismatch between how we are designed to live and how we actually live. Exercise may be one way of answering its call.

A version of this post appears on my Substack.

item.title: How Emotions Shape Our Impressions of Others
item.description:
Bias

How Emotions Shape Our Impressions of Others

The psychology of stereotypes and what they mean for all of us.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Stereotypes are the byproduct of how people think and learn.
  • When these categories are charged with emotions, they can influence behavior.
  • Understanding stereotypes can help people make more intentional evaluations about other people.

This post was co-authored with Rebecca Schlegel, Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Texas A&M University.

What do you think of when you hear the word stereotype? This term has become highly polarizing in today’s society. It probably brings to mind ideas like social justice; diversity, equity, and inclusion training; meritocracy; oppression; wokeness; and equity. You probably have emotions about these ideas, possibly strong ones, and have attitudes about what we should do as a society about these things. But what comes to mind is probably not what psychologists mean when they study stereotypes, and people are often surprised by the role of emotions in shaping what we think about others.

Mental Categories Help People Learn and Navigate the World

When viewed through a psychological lens, stereotypes are not good or bad. They are byproducts of how people think. The human mind operates by creating categories or “bins” and using those bins to collect related information. As children learn language, for example, they might create a bin called “dogs,” and place everything that is four-legged and furry into that bin. This leads to some common errors, such as children calling a cat a “dog” because it is four-legged and furry. Typically, these errors are corrected by others (a parent explains it is not a dog, but a cat), and the categories get adjusted as children learn what information goes in what bin. This structure is critical for functioning in the world—we can enter a new situation and know what to expect because we’ve been in similar situations before. Without the category of “dog,” we would have to treat every encounter with a dog as a new experience. With the category of “dog,” we have some idea of how the animal will behave and what we should and shouldn’t do when encountering a dog, and we can talk with other people about our experiences with dogs to share information. Overall, categories help us learn faster and function better.

We use this same categorization process to make sense of the many different types of people we encounter in the world. From an early age, we learn categories and place people into those categories. We learn some bins at very young ages, such as family versus stranger. As we grow and learn, the categories are adjusted based on correcting errors and greater experience. Placing people into those categories allows us to quickly respond—children learn to treat someone in the bin of “stranger” very differently than they treat someone in the bin of “family.”

Stereotypes refer to the information and beliefs we put in the bins we have learned for groups of people. Just as people might associate the bin of “dog” with concepts like loyal or energetic, people associate bins for groups of people with different concepts. For example, people may associate the category of “football player” with concepts like “strong.” At their root, stereotypes are mental shortcuts that people use to make sense of other people just as they do with other types of categories in the world. Creating the bins and putting information in the bins is just a feature of how our brain makes sense of a complicated world.

Attitude Formation Attaches Emotions to Categories and Shapes Behavior

The challenge comes when we develop emotions about the bins we use. One person might associate the bin of “dog” with loyalty and develop good feelings about dogs, whereas another person might associate the bin of “dog” with aggression and develop negative feelings about them. In the same way, people attach good or bad feelings to bins for categories of people. This process—where an emotion is attached to a category or idea—is called attitude formation. The bin is no longer neutral—there is an emotional tag that changes how you interact with the members of that category. If the bin of “dogs” is attached to negative feelings or fear, you avoid dogs. Similarly, you are disposed to act differently toward categories of people associated with negative emotions versus groups you associate with positive emotions. These emotions can be powerful guides to behavior.

The beliefs we hold about groups of people and the emotional responses we have toward the groups are different concepts in psychology. In daily life, however, these things often go hand in hand and are influenced by the messages we receive about groups. Societal views of smoking and smokers in the United States are an excellent example of how stereotypes (and the emotions they evoke) develop and can shift. From the 1920s through the 1960s, smoking was associated with glamor and wealth. This was the result of marketing by companies and striking images of celebrities in movies, ads, and television. Smoking was not only socially acceptable; it was a good thing—part of being a productive and engaged member of society. The group “smokers” had become associated with positive beliefs and positive emotions.

Man choking on smoke
Source: Mr. Exen / Shutterstock

As the health consequences of smoking behavior and the resulting economic impact became clear, government officials took steps to change public perceptions of smoking. They banned cigarette advertisements, promoted anti-smoking campaigns, and prohibited companies from using terms that suggested particular brands were safer or healthy. Many of the campaigns were graphic and evoked strong emotion, such as images of smokers with cigarette burns in their clothes and yellowed teeth, diseased lungs, or people in wheelchairs struggling to breathe. These messages were not just providing information to people about the health risks—they were actively attempting to shift the stereotypes of smoking and smokers. Over time, “smokers” became associated with negative emotions and beliefs, and were viewed as dangerous, irresponsible, selfish, unhealthy, and disgusting. They were banned from restaurants, airplanes, workplaces, campuses, and stores.

In current society, there is a high level of concern and attitudes about stereotypes and what we should do about them. Stereotypes have become a focus of political debate and calls to action. However, from a psychological perspective, stereotypes exist because they are a byproduct of how people learn, think, and navigate a complex social world, and they cannot be removed. But we can understand how messages through advertising, media, and other sources affect the impressions we form about other people. Understanding how our impressions are formed can help all of us make more intentional evaluations about other people based on our own experiences and our personal values.

item.title: How a Freak Flood Revealed the Gut-Brain Axis
item.description:
Gut-Brain Axis

How a Freak Flood Revealed the Gut-Brain Axis

After a flood, people in Walkerton, Canada, got IBS—and depression.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • A flood in Walkerton, Canada contaminated the water and sickened an entire town.
  • This was an early example of the gut-brain axis in action.
  • The microbes involved caused hundreds of people to get IBS.
  • Those with IBS also had a higher rate of depression.

“There is a tide in the affairs of men, which taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.” —William Shakespeare

In May 2000, the Canadian town of Walkerton was flooded after a heavy rain. The town’s water supply became contaminated with E. coli and Campylobacter jejuni. It was caused by overflow from a cow and chicken farm known to have problems containing their pathogens. Over two thousand of the five thousand townsfolk became seriously ill. Seven died. The town basically shut down. And then it was noticed that hundreds of these people, after recovering from their original infections, came down with IBS. They also became depressed.

Source: Midjourney

Although E. coli was present in the water, C. jejuni arguably played a bigger role in the disaster. C. jejuni is sensitive to stomach acids, which quickly killed many of the microbes. But people who regularly took antacids had lower levels of acidity, allowing more of the C. jejuni to pass through. Those using proton-pump inhibitors were twice as likely to get sick from C. jejuni.

Although diminished, many of these pathogens still made it to the intestines. These bacteria were recently inside a cow or a chicken, so they were pretty much at home in the human gut. In cows and chickens, C. jejuni is a commensal. Why it goes berserk in a human gut is unclear, but C. jejuni is potent: It is the number-one cause of diarrhea in the United States, ahead of Salmonella and E. coli. The odds are good that you’ve had it at least once in your life.

In response to C. jejuni, special cells lining the intestines secreted serotonin, which increased peristalsis in anticipation of purging.

C. jejuni caused anxiety even without a full-blown infection. Cells lining the gut called neuropods detected the invasion, causing the nervous system to go on alert before the immune system kicked in. This was an early shot across the bow; the brain now knew something was up down below.

Some heroic microbes emerged to face down the C. jejuni, including Bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus species. They worked to outcompete and crowd out the C. jejuni, preventing them from sticking to the cells lining the gut. Ironically, those who had taken antibiotics recently had lost this microbial defense and they were hit harder by the C. jejuni.

Sadly, the city officials of Walkerton insisted that the water was safe, and people kept drinking it. The C. jejuni soon overwhelmed their microbial defenses, eating through the mucus lining the gut and leaving tender gut cells exposed to infection.

Once attached to a cell, C. jejuni makes a toxin that stops gut cells from dividing. Without division, gut cells can't renew themselves and when they die, the gut lining begins to leak. A leaky gut leads to inflammation. Sure enough, the citizens of Walkerton came down with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), along with its accompanying depression and anxiety.

Stephen Collins, a professor at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, took the two-hour drive to Walkerton to see if there was a way to snatch some useful research from the town's misery.

For eight years Collins followed this group of unlucky Canadians and found that many of them had suffered intractable IBS ever since their initial infection. Collins recognized this as post-infectious IBS, which was first seen in soldiers who had picked up dysentery during World War II. About one in eight cases of IBS starts this way. Collins discovered a significant association between IBS and the mental conditions of depression and anxiety.

Intriguingly, Collins found that people with pre-existing depression had double the risk of contracting IBS. This observation underlines the dual nature of the gut-brain dialogue. It creates a positive-feedback loop, a vicious cycle that can be hard to break.

The initial infection caused the immune system to move swiftly to eradicate the offending bacteria. But in some people, the immune response failed to wind down after eliminating the pathogens, leading to treatment-resistant IBS.

Collins was joined in the research project by Premysl Bercik, also of McMaster University. Bercik took fecal matter from IBS patients and transplanted it into mice. The mice subsequently developed anxiety-like behavior, demonstrating that gut microbiota can affect mental states and that, intriguingly, those states can be transferred from one animal to another. The idea that mental states could be transmitted via fecal transplant took most scientists by surprise.

In the wake of the disaster, Walkerton erected a waterfall commemorating the victims. But the people who got IBS and became depressed started an important conversation about how the gut is related to the brain. Today, their suffering is also memorialized by the astonishing revelations of the gut-brain axis.

item.title: 100 Years of Pooh
item.description:
Friends

100 Years of Pooh

What we can learn from the legacy of Winnie-the-Pooh.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Pooh's enduring appeal includes gentle humor, recognizable personalities, and the comfort of friendship.
  • Character styles have changed little in one hundred years.
  • Transitional objects can offer comfort at any age.

A. A. Milne wrote Winnie-the-Pooh for his son, Christopher Robin. It was published on October 14, 1926, and sold 150,000 copies before the year was out. Pooh books have since sold more than 45 million copies in the United States alone, and have been translated into over 50 languages.

A Gentle World After a War

Milne was already a well-known humorist at Punch magazine and a successful playwright. Pooh himself made his first appearance in a London newspaper on Christmas Eve 1925.

Milne had served in the First World War, and Britain was still grieving. Into that world came a quiet forest where the biggest crisis was a lost tail or a bear stuck in a doorway. Pooh offered a refuge then, and he offers one now.

Friends We Recognize

Part of the pleasure is knowing these characters so well. We can almost predict what each will say. Perhaps we recognize someone we love in many of them. Perhaps, we may even recognize ourselves.

Pooh's forgetfulness is a loose match for inattentive ADHD. He may lose track of a plan, especially when honey is involved, but he never loses his affection for a friend.

Piglet approaches life cautiously. His tendency to anticipate trouble resembles the worry of generalized anxiety disorder. Yet he is loyal and willing to help. He reminds us that bravery can come in a very small package, and that feeling afraid does not stop us from doing something meaningful.

Eeyore expects disappointment. His gloom brings to mind persistent depressive disorder. But his dry humor makes him much more than the sad member of the group. His friends keep including him. He does not have to become cheerful to deserve their attention.

Tigger is movement, excitement, and impulse, much like the hyperactive side of ADHD. He can be exhausting, but he brings vitality. Most of us know someone whose enthusiasm occasionally overwhelms us, and whose absence would leave the room noticeably quieter.

Rabbit likes order and likes to be in charge, which resembles obsessive-compulsive personality traits. Owl enjoys being the expert, a playful nod to narcissistic traits, though wanting to sound knowledgeable is hardly a personality disorder.

Little has changed in terms of human characteristics in 100 years.

A Child Who Is Wise

Milne made a quietly radical choice for his time. In the Hundred Acre Wood, the child is the capable one. Christopher Robin solves problems, organizes expeditions, and reassures his anxious friends, while the animals around him are smaller and more muddled.

For young readers, this is empowering. Children spend most of their days being told what to do. In Pooh's world, they get to be the steady, kind, competent one. Perhaps that is why so many of us felt a little braver after reading these stories.

A Bear to Hold Onto

In 1953, the pediatrician and psychoanalyst D. W. Winnicott described what he called transitional objects: the beloved teddy bear or blanket that helps a young child move from total dependence toward independence. The object is comforting because it carries the feeling of being cared for even when a parent is out of the room.

Thirty years earlier, Milne took a transitional object and gave it a voice, a personality, and a whole forest. Every child who has hugged a stuffed animal at bedtime understands Pooh instinctively. In a sense, the books do for readers what the bear did for Christopher Robin. They offer comfort we can carry with us.

The Kindness of Being Included

The friends keep making room for one another. They become annoyed. They misunderstand. Their efforts to help do not always go smoothly. These trials are what make their friendships believable.

Eeyore matters here. People with depression sometimes withdraw because they believe they will bring everyone else down. Friends, unsure what to say, may pull away too. The distance grows just when connection is needed most.

We can take a gentler approach: Keep inviting. Offer a walk, a cup of tea, or a little company. Allow room for quiet. In Pooh's world, a friend is someone worth checking on.

The Wisdom of Doing Nothing

The Hundred Acre Wood offers a different pace. There is time to visit, walk, wonder, and become absorbed in something small. A modest adventure is enough to fill the day.

In 1982, Benjamin Hoff's bestseller The Tao of Pooh presented the bear as a model of simple, present-moment living. Long before mindfulness became a wellness trend, Pooh was savoring honey, noticing the weather, and enjoying his friends without needing to accomplish anything.

The Pull of Nostalgia

The word nostalgia was coined in 1688 by a Swiss physician who considered it a disease of homesick soldiers. Nostalgia tends to lift mood, strengthen our sense that life has meaning, and remind us that we are loved. In one study, people who felt lonely drew on nostalgic memories to restore their sense of connection. Looking back, it turns out, can help us move forward. The original stuffed animals that inspired Milne now live at the New York Public Library, where they receives 750,000 of visitors every year.

The Real Boy in the Story

The last lesson, and it is a sober one. The real Christopher Robin did not always enjoy being famous. As he grew older, he was teased at school, and as an adult he wrote with mixed feelings about the boy in the books. His father eventually stopped writing about him, explaining that his son had "already had more publicity than I want for him."

A Promise Kept

These stories hold the wish to be known, accepted, and remembered. Near the end of The House at Pooh Corner, Christopher Robin asks Pooh to promise he won't forget him, "not even when I'm a hundred."

Pooh's answer is simple: "I promise."

A century later, we have kept that promise too.

item.title: The Unretirement Movement
item.description:
Aging

The Unretirement Movement

Many older Americans are returning to the workforce.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Money is the primary motivator for "unretirement."
  • The desire to stay busy or engaged is another reason to unretire.
  • Due to their experience, baby boomers have much to contribute to the workplace.

More people of a certain age are holding jobs rather than waiting for their Social Security checks to arrive in the mail. The demographics of the American workforce are changing, and for the better, as it becomes more diverse in terms of age.

A 2026 AARP survey of adults age 50 and older found that over six months, 7 percent of retirees “unretired,” meaning they reentered the labor force. Not surprisingly, most of them reported that their primary reason for returning to work was to make money.

Financial problems most commonly push retirees back into the workforce: Spiraling healthcare costs or a health-related emergency are primary reasons that retirees return to work either part-time or full-time. Recent inflation spikes have also driven many older Americans to look for work, as the rising cost of living has reduced spending power. What might have seemed like a sizable nest egg has shrunk for many Americans, and the thought of running out of money is understandably terrifying.

Purpose, Structure, and Social Connection

Not just financial necessity but simply wanting to stay busy or engaged is behind the unretirement movement. While money is the major factor in returning to the workforce in some way, many retirees have found their post-career lives are not the nirvana they had expected. Americans as a whole have a strong work ethic, and full-time leisure is not as fulfilling or rewarding for those who have been productive for decades. Research indicates that engaging in work provides routine, purpose, and social connection, which can boost physical and mental well-being.

A growing labor shortage in many industries may help drive the unretirement movement and options for retirees who prefer to work on their own terms. Older adults are, among many other things, selling health insurance, becoming real estate agents, tutoring and substitute teaching, and working in retail or food service in their spare time.

Our knowledge economy also allows retirees to leverage the skills and wisdom they have gained over the years by serving as life coaches, youth mentors, community outreach specialists, and caregiving companions. According to Pivoters, which connects people over age 55 with employers looking for experienced talent, the United States has more than "100 million people 55 and over, most of whom need to work for financial reasons and want to work for the longevity, health, and social benefits of work.”

Baby boomers, now in their 60s and 70s, are not surprisingly leading the unretirement movement. In their book The Talent Revolution: Longevity and the Future of Work, Lisa Taylor and Fern Lebo examine the gradual sidelining of boomers in the American workforce. In the 1980s and 1990s, boomers were undoubtedly an economic powerhouse; however, a couple of decades later, society thinks they have little to contribute. The authors argue that digital technology created a false perception of this generation as obsolete—akin to viewing them as beta-max. The authors see older adults as essential to the future workplace, and longevity may pave the way for the coming “talent revolution.” “We identify boomers as revolutionaries—a population of disruptors that is altering career patterns, creating new expectations, and demanding inclusion,” they write.

Pairing Older Workers’ Wisdom with Younger Workers’

Chip Conley has conceived perhaps the most compelling and welcoming workplace scenario for older adults. The notion of modern elderhood has been simmering for some time, but Conley has shown how it could serve as a platform for age-friendly work. In his early 50s, Conley sold his business and wasn’t sure what to do next when he unexpectedly found a new gig as the designated “elder” for Airbnb, the online vacation rental marketplace. At that company, like most tech-driven ones, digital intelligence was the primary job qualification, putting young people with little managerial experience in major positions of power.

Conley wrote in his book Wisdom at Work, "Here exists a generation of older workers with invaluable skills—high emotional intelligence, good judgment born out of decades of experience, specialized knowledge, and a vast network of contacts—who could pair with these ambitious millennials to create businesses that are built to endure.” Conley advised older workers to repurpose their experience by seeking recognition as wise elders in organizations, like village elders in traditional societies who wielded authority based on the wisdom that came with age. Wise words indeed.

item.title: How to Set Boundaries Without the "Who Started It" Fight
item.description:
Boundaries

How to Set Boundaries Without the "Who Started It" Fight

We each remember conflict differently. You can protect yourself anyway.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • People in conflict often remember the same event very differently.
  • Fights tend to escalate when frustration builds over time.
  • You can set a boundary without agreeing on the past.

Often, when a client sits down on the couch and wants to tell a recent story about a relationship, they go back. Sometimes way back, even decades. The current event is just another brick in a wall that the client seems to carry on their back wherever they go.

In a way, it makes sense. If you want to solve a problem, it is only reasonable to track it to its beginning, take care of the roots, and let the rest follow. But the reality of relationships is often much more complicated than that. Our memories differ, and each person in the relationship often holds a different story close to their heart and can swear it is the only real truth. At times, these stories are only somewhat different, and at other times they are completely contradictory.

The Stories We Tell About Ourselves

In research about interpersonal conflict, Baumeister and his colleagues explained that "Autobiographical narratives… can be considered as the product of negotiation between actual events and desired self-concepts." That is, regardless of whether we perceive ourselves as the victim or the perpetrator in a given situation or relationship, "people can be induced to act in ways that at least mildly contradict their preferred beliefs about themselves. Rather than regarding these incidents as proof that they are immoral, weak, gullible, or otherwise lacking in virtue, people may rationalize the events by constructing stories that are more compatible with their preferred views of themselves."

This rationalization might help us build a story about ourselves, the relationship, and life that we can live with, but it won't necessarily help us thrive. While we might feel that we have a good understanding of the story, how it started and who did what to whom, the other side of the relationship might hold an entirely different one.

Same Fight, Two Different Timelines

In Baumeister's research, participants were asked to write about a time when they made someone angry and about a time when someone made them angry. When people wrote from the victim's perspective, they described the other person's behavior as arbitrary and hard to understand, and they added the event to a longer chain in the history of the relationship. When people wrote as the perpetrator, they described their own behavior as reasonable and framed the event as single and closed. The researchers suggest that conflicts often arise when one side holds in their anger and accumulates frustration over time until they eventually react, while the other person only experiences the explosion and sees it as an out-of-proportion reaction.

Waiting for Permission

Often, we are waiting for permission, from ourselves or from the people around us, to set a boundary that will protect us. We hold on to our story, telling and retelling it, because we think this is what will allow us to draw the line, to step back, to stop negotiating.

But we don't have to. We can set our boundaries without waiting for an external, objective verdict that will never come and use our internal strength and judgment to decide what we are willing to accept from other people and how to protect ourselves when the line is crossed. It doesn't have to depend on the past.

What to Ask Instead

Instead of asking "Who started this?" you can ask "What do I need right now to feel safe in this relationship?" or "What am I no longer willing to do?" These questions don't require the other side to approve your version of the story or to allow you to act as you think is appropriate.

When the Past Still Matters

That being said, this doesn't mean that the past has no meaning, or that the history of the relationship isn't affecting what it is now. You can take history into account, remember things, and still act in the present without full resolution.

Sometimes, it might be helpful to let go of the origin story and stay in the present. You don't have to ask for permission or prove you were a victim. You are allowed to set your boundaries.

item.title: Finding Your Way: Signage Still Matters
item.description:
Cognition

Finding Your Way: Signage Still Matters

Why effective signage is more important than you may think.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Both indoors and outdoors, signage can play a significant role in supporting the activities of everyday life.
  • People assume indoor wayfinding is easy, but complex environments such as hospitals challenge our abilities.
  • Designers need to devote more attention to wayfinding, but we need to be more observant of our surroundings.
Arrow to Restroom
Source: Ann Sloan Devlin

Two recent encounters with wayfinding problems reinforce my belief that good (that is, effective) signage still matters. With the advent and dominance of GPS systems and mobile apps, some people think that being able to find your way is a snap. It isn’t, especially when you are on foot.

Problems With Signage in the Community

Consider this outdoor example from my hometown. I was in my bank parking lot, which borders a busy street, and a woman across the parking lot called out, “Excuse me, can you tell me where the restrooms are?” At first I couldn’t imagine what she meant, but then she continued. “They told me the restrooms are next to the parking lot,” and then she pointed away from where we were standing and down the street. I surmised that she had asked someone waiting in a long line to get into a popular local bakery and was directed to the public restrooms, which do in fact exist and are adjacent to one of two parking lots nearby. There was a restroom sign posted on the street, but it was difficult to see amidst what I will call “signage clutter,” and the arrow on the sign wasn’t easy to make out. I walked over to her and pointed down the street, to the brick restrooms adjacent to the entry to a museum parking lot (see photo).

In this case, her wayfinding problem was solved by assistance from a human being (me) with knowledge of the area. As we all know, human beings with wayfinding knowledge are not always available.

Problems With Indoor Signage

Let’s take an indoor case. Many wayfinding problems occur in healthcare facilities (and a lot of other places, such as office buildings). A major reason for such problems is that the rabbit warren of corridors in those buildings and the complexity of the structure make providing adequate signage for all possible destinations a real challenge. Doing so can result in information overload (i.e., too much information to process). Typically, hospitals have a repetition of elements (e.g., corridors) that look the same, and the building sections have grown incrementally, often into a shape that would not have been recommended for ease of navigation. Thus, while general hospitals may have been planned to create legible (i.e., understandable) spaces, their pattern of growth often creates spatial configurations that are hard to support with signage.

In the current example, I was visiting a relative who had undergone a knee replacement, and when I entered the lobby, the receptionist handed me a piece of paper that said:

FROM THE MAIN LOBBY ENTRANCE

  • Procced straight down the hallway.
  • At the end of the hallway turn LEFT to the GREEN elevators.
  • Take the GREEN elevator to the 4th floor.
  • Exit the GREEN elevator and turn LEFT.
  • Turn LEFT again, the patient care unit 4.2 will be on your RIGHT.

As an environmental psychologist and someone who focused on wayfinding earlier in my career, I had to shake my head when handed this piece of paper. If the signage in healthcare facilities were really good, would we need these paper aids? Yet, in all fairness to the facilities, there are many people who need such assistance (e.g., people with memory problems). It is also the case that people visiting healthcare facilities are generally anxious, even if just visiting, which decreases memory function.

Signage Can Save Lives

You may be thinking, "What's the big deal? It's just a minor inconvenience to have to ask for directions to a restroom or in a hospital or to avoid being late for an appointment." But the consequences of effective signage can be far more important.

In 2016, a woman named Laura Levis having an asthma attack died outside a hospital emergency room in Massachusetts when she could not find an open entrance. As a result of this tragedy, what is known as Laura’s Law became signed legislation in 2021. Its goal is to address the need for effective signage in hospitals, and the Department of Public Health in Massachusetts is charged with implementing statewide standards for improving lighting, signage, wayfinding, and other elements connected to patient access to emergency rooms in Massachusetts. As soon as an individual is on the hospital campus, directional signs to the ER must be available (Dwyer, 2023).

Wayfinding Systems Are an Afterthought

Wayfinding systems often have been viewed as an after-the-fact application—in other words, something that is overlaid on the environment after the structure is complete (Devlin, 2014). And while we may eventually have mobile applications widely available in indoor environments for wayfinding use in hospitals, that is not currently the case (Morag & Pintelon, 2021), although a number of hospitals, including Johns Hopkins and Boston Children’s Hospital, use digital wayfinding. Such mobile applications for wayfinding are more common in commercial environments. Johns Hopkins notwithstanding, you are more likely to currently find wayfinding support such as electronic directories and interactive kiosks in healthcare environments.

NYC "Directions"
Source: Ann Sloan Devlin

And if you need convincing that signage is an afterthought, consider this example from NYC (see photo, left).

Relying on Technology to Find Our Way: Is There a Cognitive Cost?

It is clear we are headed in the direction of increasing reliance on technology to help us find our way. But is there a cost in terms of our cognitive function? For example, is there a negative impact of GPS on spatial cognition? Some cross-sectional research by Dahmani and Bohbot (2020) suggests that people who have a greater lifetime experience using GPS perform more poorly when asked to do a wayfinding task without the use of GPS. Moreover, in a small follow-up (i.e., longitudinal) study, those who had greater reliance on GPS since the first data collection showed a greater drop-off in spatial memory that depends on the hippocampus. Yet we shouldn’t jump to the conclusion that GPS use has a necessary negative impact on actual wayfinding skill. While a 2024 meta-analysis of 23 studies (Miola et al., 2024) showed a negative association of environmental knowledge with GPS use and also a negative association with self-reported sense of direction, there was no statistically significant association with wayfinding performance.

The Importance of Looking Around

As we become more and more absorbed by our technological devices for wayfinding such as smartphones and their mobile apps, we should not forget the value of simply looking around our environment. Yes, designers need to devote more time and energy to creating effective wayfinding systems, but there is great value in visually engaging with our surroundings. Not only will this likely result in better wayfinding experiences, but it will also remind us that our surroundings have the capacity to surprise and fascinate us. We have to look around to know that.
