item.title: Developing a Self-Talk Playbook
item.description:
Self-Talk

Developing a Self-Talk Playbook

Using self-talk to improve performance.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Self-talk can help us accomplish tasks, focus, and get motivated.
  • There are essentially two kinds of self-talk linked to performance: instructional and motivational.
  • Effective self-talk takes practice, but the payoff extends to virtually every aspect of life.
Motivational self-talk is a powerful performance tool.
Source: Tumisu / Pixabay

We talk to ourselves all day. This self-talk helps us to accomplish tasks, focus, and get motivated. Alternately, it can defeat us, sabotage us, and keep us from realizing our potential. What we say to ourselves is powerful and key to our ability to do just about everything.

Harnessing the power of our self-talk is a great performance optimization strategy to master. It improves both our physical and cognitive performance by building confidence, improving focus and concentration, increasing motivation, decreasing negative self-talk, and managing anxiety. Additionally, it can be deployed in the moment when we need to think quickly on our feet, pay close attention, or find that extra ounce of determination.

When we speak about performance improvement or enhancement, many people assume we are talking about athletes, pilots, and other elite performers. It’s true that elite performers are trained in the gambit of mental skills. However, these same psychological or mental skills are foundational for all of us. So—yes, self-talk can improve your professional tennis game, but it can also help to improve your attention, concentration, and emotional regulation; increase your motivation; and direct your energy toward essentially anything. So, whether you want to motivate yourself to do the dishes, get your application together for law school, improve your golf game, or ace flight training, self-talk is key.

Essentially, there are two kinds of self-talk linked to performance: instructional and motivational. They both serve to improve our performance, but in different ways. What follows is a basic guide to performance-enhancing self-talk and the information needed for you to develop your own self-talk playbook.

Instructional Self-Talk

Instructional self-talk is what it sounds like. You walk yourself through a task or problem, often with the help of a memory aid such as a mantra or acronym, or provide yourself a simple reminder cue as to how to do something. These strategies allow you to focus on the current situation or task at hand, develop effective habits related to that specific task, and ensure that you follow correct procedures. Instructional self-talk is particularly powerful when learning a new skill, during an emergency, or when having to execute a complex task.

Most of us remember learning how to use a fire extinguisher through the use of the acronym PASS (Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, and Sweep from side to side). Using the acronym more easily allows us to focus on the steps, execute the steps correctly, and gain self-control in an emergency situation. Likewise, if you’ve ever played sports, you’ve learned cues to remind you of the most effective ways to execute movements and plays.

Professions that involve high-risk and high-demand situations capitalize on instructional self-talk. Pilots and flight students, for example, know that during an emergency or task overload in the cockpit, to fall back on "Aviate, Navigate, Communicate" and then rely on the next checklist. Instructional self-talk improves cognitive and physical performance by providing direction, focusing attention, improving concentration, and helping to manage emotions.

Some simple rules of instructional self-talk include focusing on what to do, as opposed to what not to do, and keeping it relatively short and task-focused. During an emergency or if anxiety has crept in, taking one diaphragmatic breath can provide the pause you need to access your instructional self-talk and stay on track.

Motivational Self-Talk

Motivational self-talk is also what it sounds like. You increase your focus, drive, and confidence in your own abilities to accomplish the task at hand, be that getting up off of the couch to go for a walk or instilling confidence in yourself during a high-stakes sporting event or training evolution. Motivational self-talk is best used in situations in which you need an extra dose of determination, or for an already mastered skill to enhance attentional control during execution of a task.

Studies have shown that for enhancing emotional regulation, third-person self-talk is more effective than speaking to yourself in the first person. Thus, “You got this!” may be a more effective example of motivational self-talk than “I got this!”

What motivational self-talk will work for you? Ask yourself, What would I say to a good friend who is in this same situation as I am? We tend to be kinder to our friends than to ourselves, and this allows us to better focus objectively on the task, making this an effective way to find exactly what you need. So: You can do this! Let's go! You have trained for this moment and are ready. Keep moving. (You get the idea.)

In conclusion, whether you need motivation to get started, the determination to keep going, or instructional cues to navigate a challenging task, self-talk is a powerful performance tool that is available anytime, anywhere. Like any mental skill, effective self-talk takes practice, but the payoff extends to virtually every aspect of your life. Start building your self-talk playbook by identifying a few simple instructional cues for important tasks and motivational phrases that work for you. Practice them, refine them, and put them to use. After all, if you're going to talk to yourself all day, you might as well make the conversation productive.

item.title: 3 Real Ways to Evolve Past Your Trust Issues
item.description:
Relationships

3 Real Ways to Evolve Past Your Trust Issues

Trust is fragile. But it is also reparable. Use these 3 steps to begin.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • A lack of trust can lead to emotional distance, misunderstandings, and even the breakdown of relationships.
  • To begin trusting others, start by honoring your word to yourself.
  • To build trust with others, you must first learn to fully accept and love yourself.
Source: Pavel Danilyuk / Pexels

Trust forms the basis of all our connections. When trust is strong, relationships flourish, communication is transparent, and individuals feel safe and valued. On the other hand, a lack of trust can lead to emotional distance, misunderstandings, and even the breakdown of relationships.

Despite the pivotal role of trust, many people struggle to place their faith in others, often due to past betrayals. These experiences of disappointment can create a reluctance to trust new people, forming a barrier in the development of meaningful relationships. A study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology underscores how trust influences memory. People with low trust in their partner tend to recall the partner’s mistakes negatively, emphasizing self-protection over relationship dependence. Conversely, those with high trust exhibit a positive bias when remembering their partner’s transgressions.

However, letting fear dictate our ability to trust can hinder personal growth and prevent the development of meaningful relationships.

While we cannot control the betrayals of others, there are actions we can take proactively to develop a robust understanding and sense of trust so that we can be generous yet mindful the next time we decide to trust someone with it. Here are three.

1. Stop Breaking Promises to Yourself

Distrust in others often arises when you repeatedly break your own commitments. Think about it: If you can’t trust yourself to keep the promises you make to yourself, how can you trust others to keep their promises to you? To begin trusting others, start by honoring your word to yourself.

  • Set achievable goals and commitments for yourself. This will not only boost your self-confidence but also give you a track record of keeping promises, even if they are just to yourself.
  • Creating an accountability system is a potent tool for building self-trust. Share your goals and commitments with a trusted individual who can provide support and encouragement. Alternatively, keep a journal or use productivity apps to monitor your progress.

2. Work on Fully Accepting Yourself

Another source of the fear of trusting others is the dread of judgment and criticism. What you fear others might critique about you often mirrors your self-criticism. Low self-esteem and self-doubt can hinder trust in others. To build trust with others, you must first learn to fully accept and love yourself.

  • Practice self-compassion. Be kind and forgiving to yourself, just as you would be to a close friend. Acknowledge that nobody is perfect and it’s OK to make mistakes or have imperfections. This breaks the cycle of self-criticism and judgment. Research indicates that self-compassion not only helps individuals handle challenging situations but also extends its beneficial effects to elevate the enjoyment of positive events.
  • Challenge negative self-talk and replace it with positive and affirming thoughts. Our internal dialogue plays a significant role in our self-esteem and our ability to trust others. This gradually builds a more positive self-image and a healthier self-concept.
  • Celebrate your strengths and individuality. Embrace the things that make you uniquely you. This makes it easier to value yourself and extend that trust in your own worth to others.

3. Learn to Trust by Actually Trusting

It’s easy to remain guarded and skeptical, but trust cannot be developed without taking the risk of trusting others. Trust is a two-way street that requires effort and vulnerability. Here’s how you can start trusting by actually trusting:

  • Take the leap and be authentic. Authenticity is the foundation of trust because it shows that you’re not hiding behind a facade. When you are genuine, others are more likely to reciprocate by being genuine with you.
  • Understand that trust is a gradual process. Trust is not built overnight. It takes time to develop and strengthen. Research supports the idea that building trust gradually is more effective than attempting to establish trust in a single encounter. So be patient and give yourself and others the time needed to demonstrate trustworthiness. Be open to the fact that trust evolves, deepens, and becomes more resilient over time.

While you are at it, be prepared for the possibility of disappointment. Not every person or situation will result in a positive outcome. Instead of dwelling on disappointments, view them as learning experiences that can refine your judgment in the future and be open to the potential for trustful connections.

Trust is the bedrock of any healthy relationship, but fear often prevents us from placing our faith in others. Building self-trust is an incremental process; it won’t happen overnight. But by taking proactive steps, you can break down the barriers that keep you from forming deep and meaningful connections. Building trust is a journey, and the rewards of stronger, more fulfilling relationships are well worth the effort.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.
